scenes.text: Here's the knee we finished on, straight at one hundred and eighty degrees, then bending to ninety in a squat. Your hip bent too, but not in the same way. Sitting down, lift one foot and turn your whole leg so your toes point in, then out. Now straighten that knee, hold your thigh still, and turn only your shin. You'll get almost nothing. That isn't strength or flexibility. It's the shape of the bones where they meet.

The skeleton has five jobs, and only one of them is movement. It supports the body. It protects: the cranium around the brain, the vertebrae around the spinal cord, and the ribs around the heart and lungs. It makes movement possible, because bones act as levers and joints act as fulcrums, the pivots they turn on. It makes blood cells in red marrow. And it stores minerals, mainly calcium. Those last two show that bone is alive. It rebuilds to match its load, which is called Wolff's law. Load a bone and it gets denser. Remove the load, as in months in space, and it thins.

An adult has two hundred and six bones, and you need the major ones, in two groups. The axial skeleton is the central core: the cranium, the vertebral column, the ribs and the sternum. It mostly protects. The appendicular skeleton is the limbs and the girdles that attach them, and it mostly moves. In the arm, that's the clavicle and scapula, the humerus, then the radius and ulna. The radius sits on the thumb side. In the leg, it's the pelvis and the femur, the patella, or kneecap, then the tibia and fibula. The tibia carries your weight.

Now the joints, where bones meet. Every joint sits on one trade-off: mobility, how far it can move, against stability, how well it resists being forced out of place. No joint can have the most of both. Fibrous joints, like the sutures in your cranium, are knitted together by tough tissue and don't move at all, which is what you want around a brain. Cartilaginous joints, like the discs between vertebrae, have a pad of cartilage. Each moves only a little, but twenty-three of them in a row let your spine bend and still guard the spinal cord. Synovial joints have a fluid-filled gap, so they move freely.

Here's the classic exam trap. The shoulder and the hip are both ball-and-socket joints. But the hip's socket is deep, and wraps around the ball at the top of the femur. The shoulder's socket is shallow, more like a saucer. So the shoulder is the most mobile joint in the body, and the major joint that dislocates most often, while the hip is stable enough to carry your weight. Same type, opposite settings. To explain range or injury risk, look at bone shape first, then ligaments.

A typical synovial joint has six parts. Articular cartilage caps each bone end, so friction is tiny and shocks are absorbed. It has no blood supply, so it heals poorly. The joint capsule is a tough sleeve around the joint, and its lining, the synovial membrane, makes synovial fluid, which oils the joint and feeds the cartilage. Ligaments join bone to bone and stop movement in unsafe directions. Tendons, which join muscle to bone, are different. And bursae are small fluid sacs that cushion where a tendon slides over bone.

Synovial joints come in six shapes, and the shape of the bone ends decides which movements exist. A hinge, like the elbow, knee or ankle, bends and straightens in one direction. A ball-and-socket, like the hip, moves every way, including rotation. A pivot turns around one axis, like the radius rolling over the ulna. Gliding joints, between the small bones inside the wrist and the ankle, slide a little. A condyloid joint, like the wrist joint itself, where the radius meets those small bones, moves four ways but doesn't rotate. And a saddle joint, at the base of the thumb, adds the thumb's reach. So your hip turns because it's a ball and socket, and your straight knee barely does because it's a hinge, which only allows a little rotation when bent.

Now the words for movement. Every action is described from the anatomical position: upright, facing forward, arms by your sides, palms forward. Flexion decreases the angle at a joint, and extension increases it. Abduction moves a limb away from the midline, and adduction brings it back. Rotation turns a limb around its long axis. Pronation turns the palm down, supination turns it up. Dorsiflexion pulls the toes up towards the shin, and plantar flexion points them down.

Now the squat. On the way down, the hip flexes, as the angle between trunk and thigh closes. The knee flexes too, as the angle between thigh and shin closes. Saying flexion twice is right, not repetitive. The ankle is where marks are lost. It doesn't just bend. It dorsiflexes, as the shin travels forward over the foot. On the way up, everything reverses: the hip and knee extend, and the ankle plantar flexes. So always name the phase.
Two things to remember. Every joint trades mobility against stability. And the joint decides which movements exist, while the muscle decides whether they happen.
Two exam questions. First. A soccer player kicks a ball. Describe the joint actions at the hip, knee and ankle of the kicking leg as it swings forward to the ball. Pause here to answer.

Here the joints don't all move the same way. The hip, a ball-and-socket joint, flexes. The knee, a hinge, extends as the shin whips through. And the ankle, a hinge, stays plantar flexed. The classic mistake is saying the whole leg flexes, when the knee is extending.
Second. Explain how the structure of the skeletal system enables movement. Pause here to answer.

Link every structure to what it makes possible. Bones are levers and joints are fulcrums, so a muscle's pull becomes movement. Joint class decides how much movement exists. The shape of the bone ends decides which actions. Cartilage, fluid and ligaments keep it smooth and safe. And bone remodels with load. The classic mistake is a labelled list of bones with nothing about movement.

So, to describe any movement, name the joint, its type, the action and the phase. Now hold the squat at the bottom. The bones and joints allow this position, but they can't produce it. Something has to be pulling.
